title: ‘Orphaned’ by floods, more than 500 Nepali children face uncertain future - Al Jazeera
description: ‘Orphaned’ by floods, more than 500 Nepali children face uncertain future  Al Jazeera
publisher.title: Al Jazeera
full_article:
Dhading; Rasuwa; Nuwakot, Nepal – As nine-year-old Ram Thakur walked uphill with his mother and dozens of others fleeing floodwaters on August 26, he looked back and saw brown water surging up.

So they started running. His mother, who had been holding his hand until then, helped him climb faster. Then, as the sounds of the swirling water mingled with the shouts of those around them, she yelled to her son: “Chhito maathi hinda, pachhaadi na-hera,” Nepali for “Climb up faster, don’t look behind.”

That’s what Thakur did, climbing higher and higher, until he finally looked back. The water was still gurgling close by, but his mother wasn’t there any more.

Nearly four weeks later, Thakur is still waiting – hoping against hope – for his mother and father. He is currently living in a government primary school turned temporary shelter house in Nuwakot district in Nepal, with 26 other children.

They are among more than 500 children living in different temporary shelter homes across Nepal’s flood-affected districts, their parents either dead or missing. Under Nepali law, a person must be missing for 12 years before they can be declared dead. The law offers an exemption from this rule during disasters, but for that, relatives need to apply to a district court for what is known as a judicial declaration of death.

So for now, Thakur and the other children live in limbo. Legally, they’re not yet orphans. But in practice, they are without their parents – and have been since the floods that killed more than 1,400 people and left at least 5,000 others missing.

A toy truck, one of many playthings provided by nonprofits for children at Nepal’s shelters who are without their parents [Jigyasa Mishra/Al Jazeera]

‘They should have come by now’

The morning of August 26 began like any other school day for Thakur. He was on his way to school with his mother about 8am when the disaster struck. Thakur’s father, who worked as a guide and driver, was at home: His work began at 10am.

Suddenly, they heard people shouting: “Daudanu, baadhi” (“Run, flood!”)

They walked, climbed and ran until Thakur was separated from his mother. Then, he was stuck on a hill for a day with 13 other people until an army helicopter came to rescue them. “I was so scared and hungry. I thought I will also die,” he said. “My school bag, which had biscuits and a lunchbox, was also gone [in the flood].”

As he sat eating dal, rice and saag – their lunch for the day – with the 26 other children at his shelter, Thakur explained that he’s confused about why his parents haven’t turned up to find him yet.

“Mummy and papa knew how to swim so they should have come by now,” he said.

A counsellor present with him said Thakur still runs into the open whenever he hears a helicopter hovering nearby, hoping his parents have been rescued.

A post-flood assessment this month by Nepal’s National Child Rights Council and the nonprofit Save the Children found that more than 1,000 children were living in temporary shelters, including more than 100 who were unaccompanied by any relatives and 439 who were without their parents but had other relatives with them, Ayush Joshi, programme director for Save the Children in Nepal, told Al Jazeera.

In all, more than 32,000 children were displaced by the floods, and officials and nonprofits are working to trace and reunite them with their families, said Leon Muwoni, in charge of child protection at UNICEF Nepal.

So far, 18 children have been reunited with their parents, Muwoni told Al Jazeera.

Bedding, relief materials and packaged food are kept inside a child-friendly shelter tent in Nuwakot [Jigyasa Mishra/Al Jazeera]

‘She does not speak to anyone’

The shelter where Thakur is currently living has eight rooms. Six of them have been set up by local nonprofits, with waterproof mats, bedding and soft toys. Workers are building bunk beds for the children. A seventh room serves as a store for rations, and the eighth as the kitchen. Most of the staff on duty are Nepal police personnel, while the rest are representatives of nonprofits. One counsellor is with them, too. All are women.

Some 100km (60 miles) away at another children’s shelter in Dhading, four-year-old Shibani Tama does not speak any more. Both her parents are confirmed dead.

Caregivers at the shelter say she barely remembers the neighbourhood she lived in or her relatives, none of whom have come for her so far. All Shibani has told the rescue team and the counsellors is that she was at school when teachers made her rush uphill with other students.

Advertisement

“She does not speak to anyone. Doesn’t let anyone comb her hair, too. Barely lets us change her clothes in two to three days after insisting,” said Yamuna Bhattarai, a caregiver at the shelter. “It is very disturbing to see her and others who are in extreme shock. All of them are in dire need of psychosocial help.”

Corn sprouts from a mud-covered storage place, alongside a toy doll in Devighat, Nuwakot district, Nepal, September 9, 2026 [Tyrone Siu/Reuters]

‘Only ones for each other now’

Many children who have lost both parents have never known how to wash their hair, change their clothes or feed themselves. Others have become responsible for younger siblings while still children themselves.

Ten-year-old Sanju Lama was going to her grandmother’s house with her two-year-old brother in Rasuwa district – the worst affected in the floods – when strangers helped them escape the flood by pulling them along. Her home was swallowed by the water. Her parents, who should have been home when the floods struck, are missing.

“Sanju gets shocked by loud sounds, even when her name is called out,” Bhattarai said. “She keeps holding her little brother’s hand tight, almost all the time. At night, she often wakes up scared.”

The young girl spends most of her day reading English poems to her little brother. “They are the only ones for each other now,” said Bhattarai.

According to UNICEF, across the affected districts, 18 schools have been destroyed and a further 20 have sustained damage, depriving children of safe spaces to learn, play and recover. Dozens of schools are located close to riverbanks in the affected areas and remain at risk. An estimated 10,000 school-age children now face an uncertain educational future.

People light candles and pray during a day of mourning for those killed in the August 26 floods in Kathmandu, Nepal, Monday, September 7, 2026 [Dar Yasin/AP Photo]

Help falling short

Nonprofits, counsellors and childcare staff at the primary schools converted into shelters in Dhading say that efforts to make children feel safe and comfortable are often falling short. Toys, books and play materials have been distributed, but very few children are actually using them. Many remain withdrawn, distracted or too overwhelmed to play.

Joshi of Save the Children said the group had distributed toys and study materials to children in shelters. In some cases, he said, volunteers have seen children whose parents are missing “making and setting up families with parents in the dollhouses”.

“These children probably don’t even understand what exactly has happened or why,” he said. “They are clueless about the next day, and the future in totality.”

In many cases, children are now living in overcrowded shelters with little privacy. At the same time, authorities and nonprofits say they need to be careful about handing children over to people who say they’re relatives.

“Some of the children whose relatives have been located are kept in shelters if those relatives cannot provide sufficient documentation or proof of guardianship, to avoid the risks of trafficking or child labour,” said Leon from UNICEF.

Back at the shelter home in Nuwakot, Thakur sat on the front porch with an evening snack. His eyes gazed into the orange sky of the setting sun, hoping for a helicopter to arrive, carrying his parents back to him. But it was darkness that came, and it didn’t bring a chopper with it.

title: Foreign Ministers of Nepal and Portugal hold talks in New York - Khabarhub

full_article:
KATHMANDU: Foreign Minister Shisir Khanal and his Portuguese counterpart, Paulo Rangel, held a meeting in New York, the United States, on Monday.

According to Minister Khanal’s Secretariat, the meeting took place on the sidelines of the 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly at the UN headquarters in New York.

During the meeting, the two ministers expressed satisfaction with the friendly and cooperative relations between Nepal and Portugal and discussed ways to further strengthen and expand bilateral cooperation in areas of mutual interest.

The two sides also discussed making Nepal-Portugal relations more dynamic in the days ahead and advancing cooperation based on shared interests, according to Khanal’s Secretariat.

title: Asian Games: Gurung from flood-hit Nepal misses out on karate bronze - Japan Wire by Kyodo News
description: Asian Games: Gurung from flood-hit Nepal misses out on karate bronze  Japan Wire by Kyodo News
publisher.title: Japan Wire by Kyodo News
full_article:
The 22-year-old Gurung, a silver medalist at the 2022 Asian Games in Hangzhou, China, shed tears after losing in the women's 68-kilogram division on Sunday.

Gurung is one of more than 130 athletes Nepal has sent to the games.

Hopes were high for Gurung, who was named as one of Nepal's outstanding female athletes earlier in September, according to Nepalese media reports. She is from the central district of Dhading, one of the areas severely hit by massive floods and landslides on Aug. 26 that left more than 1,400 people dead in Nepal and neighboring China.

Gurung had expressed hope for her country's recovery, saying that if everyone worked hard together, the country would certainly overcome the disaster, according to the reports.

title: Nepal’s Foreign Minister Holds Flurry of UNGA Sideline Talks on First Day in New York - nepyork
description: Nepal’s Foreign Minister Holds Flurry of UNGA Sideline Talks on First Day in New York  nepyork
publisher.title: nepyork
full_article:
NEW YORK — Nepal’s Foreign Minister Shishir Khanal held a series of bilateral meetings Monday with senior officials from the European Union, Poland, Bhutan, Portugal and Japan on his first day in New York for the high-level week of the 81st United Nations General Assembly.

Khanal arrived at John F. Kennedy International Airport at 8:50 a.m. Monday on Qatar Airways Flight 703. He was welcomed by Lok Bahadur Thapa, Nepal’s permanent representative to the United Nations; Dadhiram Bhandari, Nepal’s consul general in New York; and officials from Nepal’s permanent mission to the United Nations.

Nepal’s Foreign Minister Shishir Khanal is welcomed by Lok Bahadur Thapa, Nepal’s permanent representative to the United Nations, and Dadhiram Bhandari, Nepal’s consul general in New York, after arriving Monday at John F. Kennedy International Airport to attend the high-level week of the 81st U.N. General Assembly. Photo from Shishir Khanal’s Facebook page.

After arriving in New York, Khanal said in a social media post that he was leading Nepal’s delegation during the General Assembly’s high-level week. He thanked Thapa, Bhandari and mission officials for the welcome and said he would begin a series of bilateral meetings that afternoon to advance Nepal’s priorities on the international stage.

Thapa also welcomed Khanal to New York and wished him a productive stay and successful meetings during the General Assembly.

Talks Span Europe, South Asia and Japan

Khanal began the afternoon with a meeting with Teresa Ribera, the European Commission’s executive vice president for a clean, just and competitive transition, at U.N. headquarters.

Teresa Ribera, the European Commission’s executive vice president for a clean, just and competitive transition, welcomes Nepal’s Foreign Minister Shishir Khanal for talks at U.N. headquarters in New York on Monday. Photo by Rajan Kafle for NepYork.

Khanal expressed gratitude for the European Union’s sympathy and solidarity following Nepal’s recent Bhotekoshi floods, according to Nepal’s permanent mission to the United Nations. The two sides discussed the Nepal-E.U. partnership and reaffirmed their commitment to strengthening cooperation on recovery, rehabilitation and reconstruction.

Polish Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Radosław Sikorski, and Nepal’s Foreign Minister Shishir Khanal meet at U.N. headquarters in New York on Monday. Photo by Rajan Kafle for NepYork.

Khanal then met Polish Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Radosław Sikorski at U.N. headquarters. The discussions focused on expanding Nepal-Poland relations, cooperation in areas of mutual interest and coordination at the United Nations and other multilateral forums.

According to Poland’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs, the meeting covered Poland’s support for what it described as positive political and economic changes in Nepal, including through expert assistance. The Polish ministry also said the two sides discussed Nepal’s support for Ukraine and what it described as Russia’s exploitation of Nepali citizens who are being forced to fight in Ukraine.

The Polish Foreign Ministry’s account of the meeting was posted on social media Monday. Poland has been a strong supporter of Ukraine since Russia’s full-scale invasion.

The Polish ministry later deleted that post and published a revised statement that omitted the reference to Russia’s exploitation of Nepali citizens. In its revised post, the ministry said: “The talks focused on Poland’s support for positive political and economic developments in Nepal, including expert assistance, and appreciation for Nepal’s support for Ukraine.”

In the afternoon, Khanal met Bhutanese Prime Minister Tshering Tobgay at Bhutan’s permanent mission in New York. Tobgay reaffirmed Bhutan’s solidarity with Nepal following the recent floods and conveyed best wishes for the recovery and reconstruction of affected communities.

Nepal’s Foreign Minister Shishir Khanal speaks with Bhutanese Prime Minister Tshering Tobgay during a meeting. Lok Bahadur Thapa, Nepal’s permanent representative to the United Nations, and Foreign Secretary Amrit Bahadur Rai also joined them. Photo by Rajan Kafle for NepYork.

Khanal later met Portuguese Foreign Minister Paulo Rangel at U.N. headquarters. The two officials discussed bilateral relations and areas of mutual interest.

Portugal’s Foreign Minister Paulo Rangel, right, meets with Nepal’s Foreign Minister Shishir Khanal at U.N. headquarters in New York on Monday. Photo by Rajan Kafle for NepYork.

In the evening, Khanal met Japanese Foreign Minister Toshimitsu Motegi at U.N. headquarters. Nepal and Japan marked the 70th anniversary of the establishment of diplomatic relations this year, with both countries having highlighted cooperation in areas including trade, investment, energy, infrastructure, tourism, education and culture.

Japan’s Foreign Minister Toshimitsu Motegi and Nepal’s Foreign Minister Shishir Khanal hold talks at U.N. headquarters in New York on Monday. Photo by Rajan Kafle for NepYork.

The meetings generally focused on bilateral relations and issues of mutual interest. Foreign Secretary Amrit Bahadur Rai, Thapa and other Nepalese officials also took part in the meetings.

Climate and Reconstruction on Nepal’s Agenda

Khanal is accompanied by Rai, Joint Secretary Krishna Prasad Dhakal and other officials.

Nepal is scheduled to host a side event on Sept. 25 titled “Sagarmatha to the Sea: A Call to Action for a Climate-Resilient Future.” The event will focus on climate change and its effects, particularly in the Himalayan region.

The Bhotekoshi floods are expected to feature prominently in Nepal’s discussions during the General Assembly. The disaster, which struck Aug. 26, caused extensive damage in Rasuwa, Nuwakot, Dhading and other areas along the river system. Nepal’s Foreign Ministry has described the event as an unprecedented disaster and said recovery and reconstruction will require international support.

Nepal is expected to highlight climate justice, the impact of climate-related disasters, the concerns of least-developed and landlocked developing countries, and international cooperation on investment, trade, recovery and reconstruction.

Prime Minister to Join General Assembly

Prime Minister Balendra Shah is scheduled to leave for New York on Sept. 22 and address the General Debate on Sept. 24. He is also scheduled to meet with U.N. Secretary-General António Guterres.

According to Nepal’s Foreign Ministry, Shah is scheduled to return to Kathmandu on Sept. 26, while Khanal is expected to remain in New York through Sept. 29.

The Foreign Ministry said the Nepali delegation to the high-level week includes Khanal, Rai and other senior government officials.

Pakistan’s field hockey and kabaddi teams secured their second victories at the Asian Games. In a Group B hockey match, Pakistan defeated Uzbekistan 5:1, while the kabaddi team beat Nepal 58:43, Dawn reports.

Hockey victory

The Pakistan-Uzbekistan match took place at Gifu Prefectural Green Stadium. The first half ended 1:1: Mohammad Ammad opened the scoring in the 18th minute, while Shokhrukhbek Salimjonov equalized in the 30th minute by converting a penalty corner.

After the break, Sufyan Khan put Pakistan ahead again from a penalty corner. In the 40th minute, Abdul Rehman extended the team’s lead, Abu Mahmood scored from a penalty, and Sufyan Khan completed his brace in the 57th minute. It was Khan’s third goal in two matches of the tournament. In their opening match, Pakistan thrashed Thailand 9:0, and the team’s next opponent on Thursday will be China, which defeated Thailand 8:1.

More current news is available on the UA.News Telegram channel Telegram.

Kabaddi, fencing and equestrian sport

In Kabaddi Group B, Pakistan led Nepal 30:17 at halftime. The team, captained by Mudassar Ali, eventually won 58:43. Pakistan’s defense recorded six all-outs, while the team’s raiders earned eight bonus points. Pakistan will play Thailand on Wednesday.

Meanwhile, Pakistani fencers Baryal Khan and Mohammad Yasin Khan lost all five bouts in the men’s individual foil tournament. In the individual dressage phase of eventing, Usman Khan on Eden du Veret finished 19th among 32 participants with a score of 36.70 penalty points, or 63.33%.

Soft tennis setbacks

In soft tennis, Eradj Zaidi and Kainaat Shalwani lost two singles matches each by a score of 0:4. In the men’s tournament, Mohammad Ali and Hussain Arain also lost all their matches without winning a single game.

title: Nepal-Japan festival to mark 70 years of diplomatic ties - The Kathmandu Post
description: Nepal-Japan festival to mark 70 years of diplomatic ties  The Kathmandu Post
publisher.title: The Kathmandu Post
full_article:
A special cultural festival will be held in Kathmandu on November 22 to mark 70 years of diplomatic relations between Nepal and Japan, according to the organisers.

The “Nepal-Japan Festival 2026: Solidarity Through Culture” will be held at Durbar Marg and is being organised by the Executive Committee for the Nepal-Japan Festival 2026.

According to a press statement issued by the committee, the festival will seek to highlight friendship, compassion and solidarity through Nepali and Japanese music, culture and people-to-people engagement.

A major attraction will be a performance by Japanese band Godiego, which will return to Nepal more than four decades after performing at Dasharath Stadium in 1980.

The organisers said the band’s return would add a symbolic connection to the longstanding cultural relationship between Nepal and Japan.

The festival will also feature performances by Nepali artists and cultural, tourism and commercial activities representing both countries, the statement said.

The organisers said that, in light of the Bhotekoshi river floods, any surplus generated from the festival after necessary event expenses would be donated to the Prime Minister Disaster Relief Fund.

title: After Hormuz, Nepal and wildfires, people want action to make polluters pay - Climate Home News
description: After Hormuz, Nepal and wildfires, people want action to make polluters pay  Climate Home News
publisher.title: Climate Home News
full_article:
Anne Jellema is executive director of 350.org; Mads Christensen is executive director of Greenpeace International; and Amitabh Behar is executive director of Oxfam International .

On Monday, global petitions with a collective total of more than 2 million signatures were presented to the United Nations, calling on governments to introduce binding mechanisms to make fossil-fuel companies and the super-rich contribute to the costs of the damage they have created.

The petition signatures were received by Selwin Hart, the UN Assistant Secretary-General for Climate Action, in New York during the UN General Assembly, sending a clear message to governments: there is no more room for excuses.

If governments are serious about resilience, energy security and protecting people from an increasingly unstable world, they must make the companies profiting from the fossil-fuel economy pay their fair share. Because the crisis we are facing is no longer some distant threat. It is unfolding in real time, and it is exposing the extraordinary costs of an economy still built around fossil fuels.

For more than six months, the Strait of Hormuz, the channel through which a fifth of the world's oil once flowed without a second thought, has been closed, contested or effectively unusable. Tankers sit at anchor. Insurance premiums have gone through the roof. Petrol pumps from Los Angeles to Lagos have felt the tremor. It has taken a war to remind the world just how much of our daily lives still rests on a single, fragile artery of fossil fuels.

At the other end of the same emergency, a glacier came down on the Nepal–China border in the last week of August. A wall of ice, rock and water tore through the Bhote Koshi and Langtang valleys. It has been described as one of the deadliest disasters in the region's modern history, unfolding in a landscape where the world's glaciers are retreating and destabilising at a pace scientists have been warning about for years.

And this came only weeks after hundreds of thousands of people were displaced — not by ice, but by fire. Europe has experienced its worst wildfire season in more than a decade. Homes have been lost across Spain, Portugal, France, Greece and the UK. Firefighters and civilians have been killed battling the blazes, while damage and reconstruction costs continue to reach extraordinary levels.

These are not separate crises. They are different expressions of a world becoming more volatile, while the fossil-fuel economy continues to generate enormous profits for those at the top and pushes the costs onto everyone else.

Communities absorbing cost

Because the crisis we are facing is no longer some distant threat. It is unfolding in real time, and it is exposing the extraordinary costs of an economy still built around fossil fuels. One thread runs through all of these events: a global economy still organised around the profits of a fossil fuel industry that has known, for decades, exactly what it was doing to the planet.

At a moment when governments are gathering in New York for the UN General Assembly to talk about security, resilience and economic competitiveness, it is worth spelling out what "security" - or the lack of it, driven by our economy’s dependence on oil - actually means this year for ordinary people around the world: 35,000 excess deaths in Europe due to heat; the highest food prices in three and a half years; $700 billion in economic losses, threatening countless jobs and livelihoods, from a war and a closed oil chokepoint whose consequences are nowhere near over.

Meanwhile the companies that extracted, refined, shipped and sold the fuel behind all of this continue to report extraordinary profits. Households are paying more for energy. Governments are spending billions on disaster response, on reconstruction, on emergency deployments of firefighters and aid. Communities are absorbing the cost of a system they didn't design and don't control. We pay. They profit.

This is not a coincidence, and it is not inevitable. It is a political choice, repeated year after year, to let the companies most responsible for the climate crisis hoard the wealth they generate while the rest of us carry the risk.

Taxes and fines needed

That is why, together with communities and campaigners in dozens of countries have spent the last three years building the case for a simple, overdue idea: polluters should pay for the damage they have caused. Not through voluntary pledges or distant net-zero promises, but through binding mechanisms, climate damages taxes, surtaxes on fossil fuel profits, and fines ring-fenced for recovery and adaptation that put real money where the harm actually is. This is how we take the profit out of destruction and protect the generations to come.

The response has told us we are not alone in thinking this. Our petitions calling on governments to make polluters pay have now gathered a collective total of over 2 million signatures from people across every region of the world.

The case for making polluters pay has moved into the mainstream

That is not a fringe demand. It is what happens when people watch a choke-point war spike their fuel bill, watch a glacier take a thousand lives, watch their own summer holidays rearranged by fire. They draw the obvious conclusion: the people who caused this should be paying for it – not profiting from it.

We hear the objection already forming: that this is not the moment, with wars underway and economies fragmenting, to burden industry further. We would say the opposite is true. If governments can mobilise trillions for war, for bailouts and for new fossil fuel infrastructure, they can mobilise the political will to tax the companies that caused this crisis.

Money for clean energy and resilience

That money can go straight to the people paying for it, through cheaper, cleaner, more secure energy, and through funding for communities on the frontline of floods, fires and glacial collapse. There isn't an excuse left. There is only a choice about where power and money go next. Every dollar we don’t spend now on adaptation, resilience and cutting emissions, we burn many times over later: on disasters we could have prevented and economies we scramble to fix too late.

This year's UNGA should be the moment that choice gets made in public. Governments arriving in New York will talk about resilience, about energy security, about protecting their citizens from an unstable world. Let them explain on the record why a fossil fuel industry that has spent decades profiting from that instability should not be the one paying to fix it so wrecking the planet no longer pays off.

The fires, floods and storms won't just go away. The system that keeps producing these disasters, and keeps paying the same companies for the privilege, will not change itself unless political leaders step up. It is on all of us to make sure they hear, as loudly as possible, that the time for excuses has run out.

title: Nepal promotes tourism in Japan, says major destinations remain open - The Tourism Times
description: Nepal promotes tourism in Japan, says major destinations remain open  The Tourism Times
publisher.title: The Tourism Times
full_article:
KATHMANDU: Nepal Tourism Board (NTB) is promoting Nepal’s tourism products in Japan, with nine Nepali tourism companies joining the board and Nepal Airlines Corporation at Tourism Expo Japan.

The participation coincides with the 70th anniversary of diplomatic relations between Nepal and Japan. NTB said Japan remains an important source market for Nepal, and the event provides an opportunity to develop new tourism products and strengthen business ties between tourism operators of the two countries.

At the expo, Nepal is being promoted as a destination for mountain, adventure, nature, cultural and wellness tourism, with offerings ranging from trekking and wildlife experiences to rafting, heritage tours and wellness activities.

NTB said Kathmandu, Pokhara, Chitwan, Lumbini, the Annapurna region and the Everest region remain fully operational and accessible despite the recent flash floods along the Bhotekoshi-Trishuli corridor.

According to the board, the floods primarily affected parts of Rasuwa, Nuwakot and Dhading, causing loss of lives, homes, businesses and livelihoods, while major tourism and pilgrimage destinations elsewhere in the country continue to operate normally.

Reiterating its message that “Nepal is open,” NTB said continued international travel to Nepal can help support affected communities, local businesses and tourism workers while recovery efforts continue.

The participating Nepali companies are Gochali Tours and Travels, Sumegh Tours and Travels, Himalayan Guides Nepal Treks & Expedition, Langtang Ri Trekking & Expedition, Ghale Treks & Expedition, Buddha Maya Gardens, Rupakot Resort, Chhaya Devi Complex (Aloft Kathmandu Thamel) and Gorkha International Travels.

A terrifying CCTV clip captured the moment a wall of water engulfed a land port along the Nepal-Tibet border in late August 2026, but footage that surfaced online weeks later, apparently showing the disaster from another angle, is inauthentic. It is a manipulated version of an old video of Gyirong Port; an analysis found defects in the circulating visual that suggest it was generated using AI tools.

"Video recorded by another CCTV at Gyirong Port, showing the flood towards China," reads a simplified Chinese X post from September 18, 2026.

It reposted a Nepali-language X post with a 24-second clip appearing to show people running away as a tower of water smashes the customs and border inspection building on the border of Nepal and China's Tibet region.

title: Manipulated clip of Nepal-Tibet border misleads online weeks after deadly floods - Yahoo
description: Manipulated clip of Nepal-Tibet border misleads online weeks after deadly floods  Yahoo
publisher.title: Yahoo
full_article:
A terrifying CCTV clip captured the moment a wall of water engulfed a land port along the Nepal-Tibet border in late August 2026, but footage that surfaced online weeks later, apparently showing the disaster from another angle, is inauthentic. It is a manipulated version of an old video of Gyirong Port; an analysis found defects in the circulating visual that suggest it was generated using AI tools.

"Video recorded by another CCTV at Gyirong Port, showing the flood towards China," reads a simplified Chinese X post from September 18, 2026.

It reposted a Nepali-language X post with a 24-second clip appearing to show people running away as a tower of water smashes the customs and border inspection building on the border of Nepal and China's Tibet region.

title: Himalayan expeditions hunker down as monsoon storm approaches - Nepali Times
description: Himalayan expeditions hunker down as monsoon storm approaches  Nepali Times
publisher.title: Nepali Times
full_article:
Autumn climbing season is in full swing but difficult weather conditions due to a deep depression from the Bay of Bengal heading towards Nepal From 24-27 September poses a danger to more than 1,000 climbers and guides below the world’s eighth-highest mountain.

Despite the catastrophic flood last month in an adjacent valley in the Nepal Himalaya, a record number of international climbers are on Mt Manaslu (8,163m) which is an ‘autumn peak’ that expeditions use to prepare and acclimatise for spring ascents on Mt Everest.

Climbers from Elite Exped on camp rotation this week before returning to base camp. Photo: ELITE EXPED

However, the season has not begun well. On 20 September, an avalanche at Camp III killed two climbers, German national Dhruba Jyoti Guha and his Nepali guide Phursemba Sherpa. Last week, 50-year-old Singaporean died during an acclimatisation descent at 6,000m, and Nepali guide Tashi Sherpa, 20, was asphyxiated by generator exhaust in his tent at base camp.

“Strong winds and relentless snowfall have forced climbers to reassess summit plans and return from Camps I and II to base camp,” writes Miles Sherpa, from the Summit Force team at Manaslu. Indeed, the incoming late monsoon storm system is expected to dump even more snow on a mountain which is already avalanche-prone.

Manaslu has garnered massive attention this season, with 480 permits issued to foreigners – more than on Mt Everest during this year’s very crowded spring season on Mt Everest. In addition there are 500 Nepali high altitude guides and support staff. The Mountaineering Division of the government collected $1.479 million in just climbing fees.

Altogether, 55 expedition teams comprising 432 male and 147 female climbers are in 11 of Nepal’s other peaks this season. Thirty four climbers from four teams are on Dhaulagiri I, while Mt Danga attracted 16 climbers from two teams. There are also climbers on Makalu I, Gangapurna West, Thorung Peak, Norbu Khang, Annapurna IV, Chamlang, Baruntse and Lamjung Himal. They are all said to be hunkering down for the bad weather forecast to start Thursday.

The first Manaslu summit of the season was on 17 September, and Expedition Operators Association team of Nepali climbers fixed ropes to the summit, opening the way for awaiting climbers. However, an avalanche the day before buried their ropes and climbing equipment.

To assess the current snow and route conditions across the mountain, experienced Sherpa teams made a trip toward Camp I, and they reported up to 80cm of snow at Camps I and II.

Meteorologists have warned of a low-pressure system that entered the east India coastline on Tuesday morning and is expected to dump heavy rain and snow in central and western Nepal over the weekend. Some forecast models have projected between 400mm and 740mm of rainfall, and blizzard conditions in the higher reaches.

Photo: ELITE EXPED

Even so, the eventual track of the storm system is still uncertain as it faces a stronger than usual westerly jet stream. A similar cyclone last year fizzled out by the time it reached Nepal.

“The priority is team safety, snowpack stability, avalanche conditions, and real-time mountain observations rather than a reliance on forecast models”, writes Halung Dorchi Sherpa, from the Summit Force team.

Because weather conditions are worsening and unclear, climbers are still trying to reach the summit of Makalu on Tuesday and Wednesday before the weather system blows in. To ensure that all teams safely summit, many climbers expect to have no rest days after their rotation to Camp III.

Dawa Sherpa, from Seven Summit Treks, writes from Base Camp, “For now, our teams are carefully monitoring the mountain, assessing conditions at every stage, and preparing to make the most of any safe opportunity that the weather provides.”

The short window of favourable weather may force climbers to attempt the summit all at the same time, creating a traffic jam on the knife-like summit ridge of Manaslu and other mountains.

The lead expedition guide, Lakpa Sherpa, shares his sentiment: “Patience is our greatest strength and the mountain will decide when the time is right.”

title: God, Fate And Nepal Catastrophe - The Times of India
description: God, Fate And Nepal Catastrophe  The Times of India
publisher.title: The Times of India
full_article:
Representative image

"Do not bring in god and fate to every discussion

Look within and realise what was your mission"

-Persian mystic Hakim Sanai

"Hai tujh se bhi laachaar tera Khuda"

Authored by:

Sumit Paul

We all know what happened in Nepal on August 26. Flash floods drastically altered the whole landscape of the tiny Himalayan nation and wreaked unprecedented havoc. Countless people, many of them being pilgrims, lost their lives. In this utter mayhem, you may have come across innumerable instances in which survivors are seen thanking their respective god, gods, deities and fate for their survival. Do we ever think that when one's miraculously saved in such a huge disaster, thanks to his god or goddess, why didn't the same egalitarian and benevolent god save the lives of other innocent people?Alexander Pope wrote, " Who sees with equal eye, as god of all/A hero perish or a sparrow fall/Atoms and systems into ruin hurl'd/And now a bubble burst, and now a world?"For thousands of years, humans have believed that disasters and catastrophes are caused by some divine agency or power up there in heaven who saves and slays people at will. This is a fatalist belief that has a false psychological cushion effect on humans. When we believe that it's all god's Lila (game), we shrug off our combined and collective responsibility to save precious human lives and the planet earth. When god is the (G)enerator, (O)perator and (D)estroyer, why should we care for the upkeep of planet earth? God will take care. This abject resignation to god and fate makes us so inert and sluggish.Anthropologists and neurologists have begun to believe that our belief in god, fate and stars prevents us from acting in a proactive manner. On the other hand, those who don't have any faith in god, stars, prayers and intangible phenomena, remain grounded and alert.The point is having a clear vision and conscience that man has to help his fellow humans during such cataclysmic episodes that jolt humanity. The acute awareness that no higher power does this, nor does it save mankind from these epochal events, helps us shelve god and fate for the time being. To quote Abdul Hamid 'Adam',— your god is even more helpless and hapless than you! Humans need to minimise their unflinching belief in god; better and saner, if we altogether reject it.Faith often makes us foolishly bold and valiant. We tend to ignore the worldly signs and insinuations that the clouds of danger are looming large and some disaster is afoot. It's a known fact that rains are particularly intense in Nepal till mid-September. Undertaking a risky pilgrimage to the treacherous Kailash mountain during the heavy rains must be avoided. Yet, people went there, assured and reassured that God would save them. Fate or destiny is a human concoction; it has actually no hold over humans.It's, therefore, time for all of us to think of the futility of such visits to the so-called 'holy' places. When it's in your capacity to save yourself and others, pay heed. Your intuition or warning is the voice of god. Listen to that. Stop attributing everything to god and fate and become a human full of rationality. Even if you reject atheism, you can still believe in god albeit with a ring of reason and prudence.
